title: Ames, Wittich, Mestrezat: heart’s rest in God — hunger for justice; refuge to mercy
source_text: XII. Juxta Gulielmum Amesium Anglum, Professorem Franekeræ, Fides est acquiescentia cordis in Deo, tanquam in authore vitae, vel salutis aeternae; id est, ut per ipsum ab omni malo liberemur, & omne bonum consequamur. Per illam autem cordis acquiescentiam intelligit actum voluntatis, quo movetur & extendit sese ad amplectendum bonum ab intellectu probatum, ut explicat ipse mentem suam in Medulla Theologiae, lib. 1. cap. 3. Ejusdem autem operis lib. 1. cap. 27. fides ab eo definitur, Virtus qua Dei fidelitati adhaerentes nitimur ipso, ut quod proponit consequamur. Amesio hac in parte consentit supra laudatus Wittichius, siquidem illo definiente, Fides est fames & sitis justitiae & acquiescentia cordis in Deo, ut fonte & authore salutis; ut ei animas nostras in angustiis & tentationibus committamus. In Theologia Pacifica, cap. 11. num. 128. Quibus affinis est fidei definitio quam tradit vir Doctissimus Joannes Mestrezatius, Verbi Divini, dum viveret Minister apud Parisienses, in Gallicis suis Homiliis: ubi fidem justificantem dicit esse perfugium peccatoris poenitentis ad Dei in Christo misericordiam.
pass_a_gloss: According to William Ames the Englishman, Professor at Franeker, Faith is the heart’s resting in God as the author of life, or of eternal salvation; that is, that through Him we may be freed from every evil and obtain every good. But by that resting of the heart he understands an act of the will by which it is moved and extends itself to embrace the good approved by the intellect, as he himself explains his mind in the Marrow of Theology, book 1, ch. 3. And in book 1, ch. 27 of the same work faith is defined by him as a Virtue by which, adhering to God’s faithfulness, we lean on Him that we may obtain what He proposes. In this part the Wittich praised above agrees with Ames, since on his definition Faith is a hunger and thirst for justice and the heart’s resting in God as the fountain and author of salvation; that in straits and temptations we may commit our souls to Him. In Theologia Pacifica, ch. 11, num. 128. Akin to these is the definition of faith which the most learned man John Mestrezat, while he lived Minister of the Divine Word among the Parisians, hands down in his French Homilies: where he says justifying faith is the refuge of the penitent sinner to God’s mercy in Christ.
pass_b_english: Ames: faith = heart’s rest in God as author of life/eternal salvation.
Will-act embracing the good the intellect approves (Marrow I.3); virtue leaning on God’s faithfulness (I.27).
Wittich: hunger and thirst for justice + heart’s rest in God as salvation’s fountain.
Mestrezat: justifying faith = penitent sinner’s refuge to God’s mercy in Christ.
